items.raw_snippet: # Meet Yang Zhilin, the CEO and founder behind China's buzzy new Kimi K3 AI model. Moonshot AI CEO Yang Zhilin speaks at a conference. Yang Zhilin, cofounder of Moonshot AI, the Chinese company behind Kimi K3, speaks at a conference in Beijing. Yang Zhilin is the 34-year-old researcher and entrepreneur behind the Chinese company Moonshot AI and its new open-weight Kimi K3 AI model, which seized Silicon Valley's attention this week. Kimi K3 is the latest buzzy open-weight model from China. Its coding and agentic capabilities rival those of leading American models from labs like OpenAI and Anthropic and come at a much lower cost, marking a new milestone for China in the AI race. "He is absolutely brilliant," Salakhutdinov said of Yang in a post on X on Friday. Before launching Moonshot AI, Yang returned to China and contributed to several major AI projects, including Huawei's PanGu model and the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence's Wu Dao, a large-scale multimodal AI model.

items.title: What SaaS Leaders Teach Every CEO About Winning ...
items.snippet: # **What SaaS Leaders Teach Every CEO About Winning the Agentic AI Revolution**....
items.raw_snippet: # **What SaaS Leaders Teach Every CEO About Winning the Agentic AI Revolution**. T**here****is a temptation to believe that the artificial intelligence revolution is primarily a technological race.**Every week a new foundation model is launched, reasoning capabilities improve, inference costs decline and another company announces an AI copilot or digital assistant. It is no longer about building the smartest AI. It is about **redesigning the firm around autonomous execution**. For the first time in its history, software is no longer simply supporting work. Because software companies are experiencing this transition before most other industries, they offer perhaps the clearest view of how every organisation will eventually need to reinvent itself. Our research on one hundred leading SaaS companies, combined with benchmarking of AI-native challengers and the development of an economic model of pricing and strategic migration, reveals that success does not depend primarily on better algorithms. It depends on five strategic reinvention plays that fundamentally reshape the firm’s organisation, business model and competitive position.
